2. The plaintiffs brought Other Class Suit No. 772 of 1977 in the second court of Munsif, Mymensingh, Sadar for declaration of their title to the suit lands described in schedules 1 and 2 to the plaint. Their case, as disclosed in the plaint is that schedule 1 land measuring 4.30 acres originally belonged to one Jagat Mohini Dasya who settled the same with the plaintiffs in 1332 B. S. and the plain-tiffs have since been in possession thereof. Their further case is that schedule 2 land measuring 2.66 acres originally belonged to All Sheikh in jote right. After his death his heirs sold the same to plaintiff Nos. 1„and 3 by two kabalas dated 2 July 1977. Since then the said plaintiffs- have been possessing the said land. In December 1974 the plaintiffs came to know that both the schedule lands have been wrongly recorded in the names of defendant Nos. 1-11 who have got no right title and possession therein. 

 4. The suit was dismissed by the trial court disbelieving the plaintiffs' case of settlement and on a finding that the plaintiffs had no possession in the suit lands. It was also held that the Assistant. Custodian of Enemy property having not been made a party to the suit, the suit was bad for defect of party. 

 7. Appearing in support of the appeal Mr. Miah Abdul Gafur, submits that the appellate court has not given an independent finding that the plaintiffs have no possession of the schedule lands. It has also not considered the evidence on record and has not adverted to the plaintiffs' contention in the appeal that the trial court's finding on possession is not correct. In such circumstances the High Court Division, it is submitted, dismissed the suit to the prejudice of the plaintiffs. The High Court Division could at best remand the case to the appellate court for fresh consideration on merit. 

 8. We are inclined to sustain arguments of Mr. Miah Abdul Gafur. The suit was found not maintainable by the trial court for want of possession of the plaintiffs in accordance with the proviso to Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The appellate court found fault with the finding of possession arrived at by the trial court holding that the reasons of the trial court suffered from discrepancy. Again, the appellate court also found that the Assistant Custodian of Vested Property was necessary for the sake of effective and complete adjudication. The appellate court thus did not give any independent finding on possession or decide the matter of impleading the Assistant Custodian in the suit itself. The said Court had sent back the case on remand for deciding it on all points after fresh trial. Such an order on the facts and in the circumstances of the case has not caused any miscarriage of justice for any patent illegality as such. It was not proper for the High Court Division while exercising revisional jurisdiction to interfere with the order of remand.
